lines: Writing meaning into a query is one thing.
Now: what happens when two different sessions try to write the same row at once.
One statement can match rows between a target and a source, and decide, row by row: insert this one, update that one, delete this other one.
Powerful. One pass, several different outcomes.

But power has a sharp edge here. If the source accidentally offers two rows for the very same target... the statement doesn't quietly pick one and move on. It raises an error, on purpose, the second time it tries to touch that row.
A silent duplicate becomes a loud failure instead. That's deliberate.
Now, the sharper edge, and the one worth sitting with.
There's an older, narrower statement that only ever does one thing: insert, or update if it's already there.
That older one makes a hard promise: one of those two outcomes always happens, no matter how many other sessions are racing it at the same instant.
Does the newer, richer statement make that same hard promise?
answer: No. And that's the whole point to remember.
The richer statement decides which branch to take by looking at a snapshot, taken a moment earlier.
If another session slips in and inserts that exact same row in the gap right after... the richer statement doesn't notice and switch branches. It just tries its own insert, and collides.
The narrow one is built, down at the index itself, to never leave that gap open. The richer one simply wasn't built that way... it trades that guarantee for being able to do more things at once.

lines: So the choice isn't "which one is better." It's "which one actually matches what you need."
Need a guarantee, with no race, for exactly one simple pattern... reach for the narrow one.
Need several branches, several kinds of action, maybe a second source entirely... reach for the richer one, and be ready to catch the occasional honest collision.
One more wrinkle, in a completely different kind of storage.
In an ordinary table, updating a row changes that row, in place.
In a lakehouse table built from files, there is no "in place." Changing even one row means rewriting the whole file it lives in.
Write a careless, catch-all branch on a statement like this, and you can quietly force every single file in the table to be rewritten... for a change that only touched a few rows.
So: a richer merge can do more, but it can still collide for real, on purpose, under real concurrency.
The narrow upsert trades flexibility for a promise that never breaks.
And on file-based storage, the same four letters hide an entirely different, heavier cost.
Every clause this section covered answers one question at a time.
